q: Jailbreak vs prompt injection?
short: A jailbreak tries to make the model violate its own safety policies; prompt injection tries to make an application's model follow attacker instructions instead of the developer's (e.g. leak data, misuse tools).

q: What is indirect prompt injection?
short: Malicious instructions embedded in content the model processes (web pages, emails, documents, tool results) rather than typed by the user, which can hijack agents that read and act on that content.
detail: Root cause: instructions and data share one channel.
example: "Email the customer list…" in a document.

q: What are guardrails?
short: Checks and policies around a model: input classifiers and restrictions, output filters (harm, PII, format), tool allow-lists and human escalation, independent of the model's own alignment.
mistakes: Relying solely on the system prompt.

q: What is red teaming?
short: Systematic adversarial testing by experts, crowds or automated attackers to find failures, measured by attack success rate per category, followed by fixes and regression tests.

q: How can LLMs leak training data?
short: By memorising sequences (especially duplicated ones) and reproducing them when prompted, enabling extraction of personal data or secrets; membership inference can reveal whether a record was trained on.
mistakes: Assuming training data can't be recovered.

q: How do you test for bias?
short: Counterfactual prompts that change only a group attribute, bias benchmark suites, disaggregated metrics by group and language, and toxicity classifiers on outputs; compare score gaps and refusal rates.

q: What is defence in depth for LLMs?
short: Layering independent protections (aligned model, input/output guardrails, least-privilege tools, confirmations, monitoring, red teaming, human oversight) so one failure doesn't cause harm.

q: 12 harmful probes, 3 succeed. ASR?
mistakes: Dividing by all probes including benign.

q: Secure a browsing agent against indirect injection.
short: Treat page content as untrusted data in delimited context, detect suspicious instructions, separate the planner from content processing where possible, restrict tools (no access to secrets, allow-listed domains), require user confirmation for side effects, and log/monitor actions.
detail: Assume the model can be fooled.
mistakes: Trusting a 'don't follow page instructions' prompt alone.

q: Why do jailbreaks keep working?
short: Safety behaviour is learned from finite examples and competes with helpfulness; capabilities generalise to novel framings faster than refusals; attackers search a huge input space (including automated optimisation).
mistakes: Believing a patch ends the problem.

q: Input vs output guardrails?
short: Input guardrails stop harmful or out-of-scope requests early (cheap) but miss attacks that look benign; output guardrails inspect what was actually generated (catch more, including injection effects) but cost latency. Use both.

q: Explain DP-SGD.
short: For each example compute its gradient, clip it to norm C, sum, and add Gaussian noise scaled to C before the update; this bounds how much any one record affects the model, giving a formal privacy guarantee (ε, δ) at some accuracy cost.

q: What is over-refusal and why does it matter?
short: Refusing benign requests that superficially resemble harmful ones; it frustrates users, pushes them to less safe tools, and signals poorly calibrated guardrails, so it must be measured alongside missed harm.

q: How does deduplication improve privacy?
short: Memorisation risk rises sharply with the number of copies; removing exact and near-duplicates reduces verbatim regurgitation and extraction success without much cost to quality.

q: Plan a red-teaming programme for a new assistant.
short: Define harm taxonomy and policies, recruit domain experts, add automated attacker models, test across languages and multi-turn settings, measure ASR per category, triage and fix, convert findings to regression tests, and repeat for each release.

q: Why can't prompt injection be fully solved with better prompts?
short: LLMs process instructions and data in the same token sequence without a hard boundary; any text can influence behaviour, so prompt-level separation is probabilistic. Robust designs limit capabilities and verify actions rather than trusting the model to ignore instructions.
detail: Analogous to SQL injection before parameterised queries.
example: Hidden instructions in a retrieved file.

q: Deploy an LLM in hiring responsibly.
short: Limit it to assistive tasks (summaries, not decisions), remove protected attributes where possible, run counterfactual and disaggregated audits, document limitations, keep human decision-makers accountable, allow candidate recourse, and comply with applicable regulation.
mistakes: Automated rejection based on model scores.

q: How do automated red-teaming systems work?
short: An attacker LLM generates diverse adversarial prompts, a target model responds, a judge classifies harm, and successful attacks are refined or mutated (RL or search) to explore new failure modes at scale.

q: Trade-offs of differential privacy for LLMs?
short: Formal guarantees on per-record influence, but noise and clipping reduce accuracy, increase compute, and are hardest for rare data; often applied to fine-tuning on sensitive data rather than full pre-training.

q: Write an incident-response plan for an LLM product.
short: Monitoring and alerting on safety signals, a reporting channel, severity triage, the ability to roll back models/prompts and disable tools quickly, root-cause analysis, user communication, regression tests, and post-incident review.
mistakes: No way to disable a tool quickly.
